title: Computer-vision task atlas: restoration, denoising, super-resolution, face recognition, medical imaging, video and optical flow
tagline: For each task: formulation, architecture, loss, metric and the trap that ruins papers.
explain:
**Classification / localisation / detection / segmentation** (see the previous concepts): classification (accuracy, top-5), detection (**mAP@IoU**; YOLO, Faster R-CNN, DETR), semantic/instance/panoptic segmentation (**IoU/mIoU**, Dice; U-Net, Mask R-CNN, SAM), pose estimation (keypoint heatmaps, PCK), depth estimation, 3-D vision (NeRF, Gaussian splatting).

**Image restoration family.** Observation $y=Hx+n$ (blur/downsample $H$, noise $n$); recover $x$.
- **Denoising**: DnCNN (residual learning: predict the noise), U-Net, Restormer/SwinIR transformers, Noise2Noise / Noise2Void (self-supervised, no clean targets), diffusion priors. Metrics **PSNR** $=10\log_{10}\frac{MAX^2}{MSE}$, **SSIM**, LPIPS.
- **Deblurring / inpainting / dehazing / deraining**: encoder-decoder with skip connections, multi-scale and GAN/perceptual losses (VGG features), mask-aware convs.
- **Super-resolution (SR)**: SRCNN → **EDSR** (residual blocks, no BN) → **SRGAN/ESRGAN** (perceptual + adversarial loss, sharper but hallucinates) → SwinIR → diffusion SR. **Sub-pixel convolution (PixelShuffle)** upsamples efficiently. Trade-off: **perception-distortion** - PSNR-optimised models are blurry, GAN models look sharp with lower PSNR.
- **Colourisation, HDR, low-light enhancement, style transfer** (Gatys: match Gram matrices of VGG features; fast feed-forward and AdaIN variants).

**Face analysis.** Detection (MTCNN, RetinaFace), alignment, **recognition**: embed faces with a CNN trained with **angular-margin softmax** (ArcFace/CosFace/SphereFace: $\cos(\theta+m)$ increases inter-class margin) and compare by cosine similarity; verification (same/different, ROC at fixed FAR) vs identification (rank-1). Also attributes, emotion, anti-spoofing. **Ethics**: demographic bias, consent, surveillance, legal limits.

**Medical imaging.** Modalities: X-ray, CT, MRI, ultrasound, histopathology (gigapixel whole-slide images), fundus, dermoscopy. Tasks: diagnosis, lesion detection, organ/tumour **segmentation** (U-Net, nnU-Net, Dice + cross-entropy, Tversky/focal for tiny lesions), registration, report generation. Realities: small labelled sets (transfer learning from ImageNet/medical SSL, augmentation), **class imbalance**, **patient-level splits** (never split slices of one patient across train/test), multi-centre **domain shift** (scanner/protocol), inter-rater variability, calibration, explainability (Grad-CAM), regulatory (FDA/CE) and external validation. Metrics: AUC, sensitivity at fixed specificity, Dice, Hausdorff distance, calibration.

**Video and action recognition.** Add time: **two-stream** (RGB + optical flow), **3D CNNs** (C3D, I3D, SlowFast), **(2+1)D** factorised conv, **video Transformers** (TimeSformer, ViViT, VideoMAE), temporal segment networks; tasks: action classification (Kinetics, top-1/5), temporal action localisation, tracking (SORT, DeepSORT, ByteTrack), video captioning/QA, anomaly detection in surveillance. Challenge: compute, long-range temporal context, sampling strategy.

**Optical flow.** Estimate per-pixel motion between frames: classic **Horn-Schunck** (brightness constancy + smoothness), **Lucas-Kanade** (local least squares); deep: **FlowNet**, **PWC-Net**, **RAFT** (all-pairs correlation volume + recurrent updates). Metric **EPE** (end-point error). Used for video interpolation, stabilisation, action recognition, SLAM.

**OCR and document AI**: text detection (DBNet) + recognition (CRNN+CTC, TrOCR), layout (LayoutLM), donut. **Remote sensing**, **autonomous driving** (BEV perception, multi-sensor fusion), **industrial inspection** (anomaly detection, PatchCore).
tradeoffs: Perceptual and adversarial losses sharpen images but can hallucinate content - dangerous in medical settings.
Heavier video models gain accuracy at large compute cost.
pitfalls: Patient or video leakage across splits.
Reporting PSNR only for SR with GAN models.
Face recognition evaluated without demographic breakdown.
interview: Why is residual learning used for denoising?
How does ArcFace improve face embeddings?
use: Pick the task formulation and metric before the architecture; start from pretrained backbones.
avoid: Never evaluate a medical model without external, patient-level held-out data.

qa.q: Why do GAN super-resolution models score lower PSNR but look better?
qa.a: PSNR rewards pixel-wise averaging (blurry mean predictions). Adversarial/perceptual losses push outputs onto the natural-image manifold with sharp textures that don't match ground-truth pixels exactly - the perception-distortion trade-off.

title: Time-series foundations: stationarity, ACF/PACF, decomposition, differencing, ARIMA/SARIMA, exponential smoothing
tagline: The statistical vocabulary you need before (and to benchmark against) deep forecasters.
explain:
**Time series** $\{y_t\}$ are ordered, autocorrelated observations: i.i.d. assumptions fail and splits must respect time.

**Components (decomposition).** Trend $T_t$ + seasonality $S_t$ + residual $R_t$ (additive $y=T+S+R$ or multiplicative $y=T\cdot S\cdot R$ - log transform converts one to the other). Methods: classical moving averages, **STL** (LOESS, robust, flexible seasonality), Prophet-style regression, X-13.

**Stationarity.** **Weak stationarity**: constant mean, constant variance, autocovariance depends only on lag. Most classical models require it. Tests: **ADF** (null: unit root ⇒ non-stationary), **KPSS** (null: stationary) - use both. Fixes: **differencing** $\nabla y_t=y_t-y_{t-1}$ (trend), **seasonal differencing** $y_t-y_{t-s}$, log/Box-Cox for variance, detrending. Over-differencing injects negative autocorrelation.

**ACF / PACF.** Autocorrelation $\rho_k=\mathrm{Corr}(y_t,y_{t-k})$; partial autocorrelation removes intermediate lags. Reading: AR($p$) → PACF cuts off after $p$, ACF decays; MA($q$) → ACF cuts off after $q$, PACF decays; seasonality → spikes at multiples of $s$; slow ACF decay → non-stationary. Ljung-Box tests residual whiteness.

**Models.** **AR($p$)**: $y_t=c+\sum\phi_iy_{t-i}+\varepsilon_t$. **MA($q$)**: $y_t=c+\varepsilon_t+\sum\theta_j\varepsilon_{t-j}$. **ARMA** combines; **ARIMA($p,d,q$)** adds $d$ differences; **SARIMA($p,d,q$)($P,D,Q$)$_s$** adds seasonal terms; **ARIMAX/SARIMAX** exogenous regressors; **VAR** multivariate; **GARCH** volatility clustering; **state-space / Kalman filter**; **Holt-Winters / ETS** exponential smoothing $\ell_t=\alpha y_t+(1-\alpha)(\ell_{t-1}+b_{t-1})$; **Theta**, **Prophet**, **TBATS**. Box-Jenkins workflow: identify (ACF/PACF) → estimate (MLE) → diagnose (residual ACF, Ljung-Box, normality) → forecast with intervals. Choose by AIC/BIC and out-of-sample error.

**Evaluation**: rolling-origin (walk-forward) validation, horizons h=1..H, **MASE/sMAPE/RMSE**, naive and seasonal-naive baselines (hard to beat!), prediction-interval coverage, Diebold-Mariano test for forecast comparison.

**Feature engineering for ML on time series**: lags, rolling mean/std/min/max, expanding stats, differences, calendar features (day-of-week, holidays), Fourier terms, target encoding by group, leakage-free windows.
tradeoffs: Statistical models are strong on small, single series with interpretable parameters; deep models shine on many related series.
Differencing makes data stationary but removes level information.
pitfalls: Random train/test split on time series.
Forecasting a non-stationary series with a stationary model.
interview: How do you decide $p$ and $q$ from ACF/PACF?
use: Forecasting baselines, residual diagnostics, preprocessing for neural forecasters.
avoid: Do not difference more than needed; do not skip diagnostics.

qa.q: A series has ACF decaying slowly. What next?
qa.a: It signals a unit root/trend: confirm with ADF/KPSS, difference once (or detrend), recheck the ACF/PACF, then pick AR/MA orders.

title: Deep forecasting: RNN/LSTM, TCN, N-BEATS, Transformers, Informer, Autoformer, PatchTST, Temporal Fusion Transformer
tagline: Architectures for long-horizon, multivariate and probabilistic forecasting, and the honest benchmark caveats.
explain:
**Setup.** Given a look-back window $y_{t-L+1:t}$ (and covariates), predict horizon $y_{t+1:t+H}$. **Strategies**: recursive (feed predictions back; error accumulates), direct (one model per horizon), **multi-output / seq2seq** (predict all $H$ at once; standard for deep nets). Always scale per series (RevIN - reversible instance normalisation fights distribution shift), use windows with stride, and validate walk-forward.

**Recurrent**: LSTM/GRU encoder-decoder, **DeepAR** (autoregressive RNN across many related series with a likelihood head: Gaussian/neg-binomial → probabilistic forecasts). Limitations: sequential training, long-memory loss.

**Convolutional**: **TCN** (causal + **dilated** convolutions, residual blocks; receptive field grows exponentially with depth; parallel, stable gradients), WaveNet; **N-BEATS / N-HiTS**: stacks of fully-connected blocks with backward/forward residual links, interpretable trend/seasonality bases - a purely MLP model that beat statistical baselines in M4.

**Transformers.** Vanilla attention is $O(L^2)$ and point-wise attention over single time steps is a weak fit.
- **Informer**: **ProbSparse** self-attention (select dominant queries by KL sparsity measure, $O(L\log L)$), **self-attention distilling** (halving sequence length per layer), generative-style decoder predicting the whole horizon.
- **Autoformer**: **series decomposition** blocks (moving-average trend/seasonal split inside the network) + **auto-correlation** mechanism (period-based dependencies discovered via FFT, sub-series aggregation).
- **FEDformer**: attention in frequency domain (Fourier/wavelet).
- **PatchTST**: split each channel into **patches** (like ViT tokens), **channel-independent** shared Transformer; longer look-back at lower cost, strong results and self-supervised pretraining.
- **iTransformer**: attention over **variates** (each series as a token). **TimesNet** (2-D periodicity), **DLinear** (a single linear layer on trend/seasonal parts - showed that many Transformers did not beat simple linear baselines on common benchmarks).
- **Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT)**: variable-selection networks, static covariate encoders, LSTM local processing, interpretable multi-head attention, **quantile outputs**; designed for multi-horizon forecasting with known/unknown covariates - interpretable.
- **Foundation models**: TimeGPT, Chronos (tokenised values + T5), Lag-Llama, Moirai, TimesFM - zero-shot forecasting.

**Training**: loss MSE/MAE/Huber for point, pinball/quantile or NLL for probabilistic; scheduled sampling; ensembling; covariates (calendar, promotions).

**Benchmark caveats for papers**: datasets (ETTh/ETTm, Electricity, Traffic, Weather, M4/M5), **fixed look-back windows and fair hyper-parameter budgets**, report MSE and MAE at all horizons, include DLinear/seasonal-naive/ARIMA baselines, check for **data leakage** (normalisation using future statistics, "drop-last" bugs) and use multiple seeds.
tradeoffs: Transformers capture long-range, multivariate structure but are data-hungry and not always better than linear baselines.
Channel-independent models are robust; channel-mixing can overfit spurious cross-series patterns.
use: Many related series, rich covariates, long horizons, probabilistic needs.
avoid: Do not use deep models on a single short series; ETS/ARIMA win.

qa.q: Why do simple linear models sometimes beat Transformers on forecasting benchmarks?
qa.a: Permutation-invariant point-wise attention loses temporal order information, and benchmark series are dominated by smooth trend/seasonality that a linear map on the look-back window captures with far fewer parameters, so large models overfit.

title: Time-series anomaly and change-point detection: forecasting-residual, reconstruction, density, CUSUM, PELT
tagline: Find the point, contextual and collective anomalies - and the moment the data-generating process changes.
explain:
**Anomaly types**: **point** (single outlier), **contextual** (normal value in wrong context, e.g. 30 °C in winter), **collective** (a subsequence abnormal as a whole). Labels are rare, so methods are mostly unsupervised/semi-supervised (train on normal data).

**Approaches**
- **Statistical**: rolling z-score / robust (median-MAD), seasonal-hybrid ESD, STL-residual thresholding, control charts (EWMA, Shewhart).
- **Forecasting-based**: predict the next value with ARIMA/LSTM/TCN/Transformer; anomaly score = |actual − forecast| normalised by the running error scale (e.g. dynamic thresholds in NASA's LSTM-based detection).
- **Reconstruction-based**: (variational/LSTM/conv) autoencoders on windows; score = reconstruction error; **USAD**, **OmniAnomaly** (stochastic RNN + VAE), **Anomaly Transformer** (association discrepancy), TranAD.
- **Density / distance**: Isolation Forest on window features, LOF, one-class SVM, matrix profile (**discord discovery** - the subsequence with the largest nearest-neighbour distance), GMM.
- **Adversarial**: GAN-based (AnoGAN, TadGAN).
- **Multivariate**: model correlations between channels (graph deviation GDN), Mahalanobis distance, PCA residual (SPE/Hotelling T²).

**Thresholding & evaluation**: pick thresholds from validation percentiles, POT (extreme value theory), dynamic/non-parametric thresholds; metrics on **events** not points - precision/recall/F1 with **point-adjust** (inflates scores - criticised), range-based precision/recall, VUS-PR, time-to-detect; report false alarms per day. Beware benchmark flaws (labels in NAB/Yahoo/SMD).

**Change-point detection (CPD).** Locate times where the distribution (mean, variance, trend) changes.
- **CUSUM**: $S_t=\max(0,S_{t-1}+x_t-\mu_0-k)$, alarm when $S_t>h$; optimal for a known shift (online).
- **Likelihood-ratio / GLR**, **Bayesian online CPD** (run-length posterior), **PELT** (exact penalised-cost segmentation in $O(n)$, minimise $\sum\mathcal C(y_{seg})+\beta\cdot\#\text{changes}$), binary segmentation, window-based discrepancy, kernel CPD (MMD), **ruptures** library. Deep: TCN/contrastive CPD.
Use: drift detection in production models, regime changes in finance, equipment degradation, A/B test monitoring.

**Concept drift** (change in $P(y|x)$) vs **data drift** (change in $P(x)$): ADWIN, DDM, Page-Hinkley, KS tests on feature windows; trigger retraining.
tradeoffs: Forecast-residual scores are interpretable; reconstruction models capture multivariate structure but can reconstruct anomalies too.
pitfalls: Point-adjusted F1 reported as if standard F1.
Threshold tuned on the test period.
interview: How would you detect anomalies in server metrics with weekly seasonality?
use: Monitoring, IoT, finance, predictive maintenance, MLOps drift alarms.
avoid: Don't use accuracy on rare-event labels.

qa.a: Weekly or daily cycles create regular highs/lows that a global threshold would flag; removing seasonality (STL/forecast residuals) leaves a stationary residual where deviations are genuinely abnormal.

title: Hybrid ML-DL models: CNN-LSTM/GRU/BiLSTM/Transformer, attention hybrids, wavelet hybrids, autoencoder-boosting, stacking and multimodal fusion
tagline: How and why to combine components, design ablations that justify the combination, and avoid 'frankenstein' papers.
explain:
**Rationale.** Each component has a different inductive bias: **CNN** (local patterns/shift invariance), **RNN/LSTM/GRU** (sequential state, short-medium memory), **BiLSTM** (both directions), **Transformer/attention** (global dependencies, parallel), **GNN** (relational structure), **tree ensembles** (tabular interactions), **classical models** (trend, interpretability), **signal processing** (wavelets, EMD, Fourier: multi-scale decomposition). A hybrid is justified only if the *problem* has both kinds of structure.

**Common patterns**
1. **CNN → LSTM/GRU/BiLSTM** (feature extractor then temporal model): CNN extracts local motifs from windows/spectrograms/EEG; LSTM models their order (activity recognition, load forecasting, ECG).
2. **CNN-BiLSTM-Attention**: add attention pooling to weight informative time steps/channels; aids interpretability.
3. **CNN-Transformer / Conformer**: local convolution + global self-attention (speech, vision, time series).
4. **Autoencoder → classifier/boosting**: AE/VAE compresses features, then XGBoost/SVM classifies; or AE for denoising/anomaly features. **PCA + SVM**, **LDA + KNN**, **feature selection (GA/PSO) + deep net** are classic ML-DL hybrids.
5. **Wavelet / EMD / VMD decomposition + DL**: decompose a non-stationary signal into sub-bands (db4 wavelets, CEEMDAN), model each with CNN/LSTM, **sum the forecasts**; popular in energy, hydrology, finance, EEG. Pitfall: decomposing the *whole* series before splitting leaks future information - decompose within each window/training fold only.
6. **Statistical + DL residual hybrids**: ARIMA/ETS for trend, LSTM on the residuals (Smyl's ES-RNN won M4).
7. **Ensembles & stacking**: average/weighted heterogenous nets; stacking with a meta-learner on out-of-fold predictions; snapshot/seed ensembles.
8. **Multimodal fusion**: **early fusion** (concatenate raw inputs), **feature-level / intermediate fusion** (concatenate embeddings; cross-attention), **late/decision-level fusion** (combine per-modality predictions: averaging, voting, learned gating). Examples: image + clinical tabular data, audio + video, text + images (CLIP), sensor fusion for driving. Handle missing modalities (modality dropout), alignment, differing sampling rates.
9. **Physics/knowledge-guided hybrids** (PINNs, grey-box models), **neuro-symbolic** systems, retrieval-augmented models.

**Designing a defensible hybrid**: (a) strong simple baselines (each component alone, plus well-tuned tree/linear models), (b) **ablation table** removing each block, (c) same tuning budget for all, (d) multiple seeds + significance tests, (e) complexity (params, FLOPs, latency), (f) show the combination wins for a *reason* (error analysis by regime), (g) release code and seeds.

**Reviewer red flags**: stacking many modules without ablation, tuning only the proposed model, leakage via decomposition/scaling, tiny test sets, "novelty" that is just a new combination of known blocks.
tradeoffs: Hybrids can exploit complementary strengths but multiply hyper-parameters, cost and failure modes.
More components rarely help when data is small.
interview: Why a CNN before an LSTM for sensor data?
How would you show each block of your hybrid matters?
use: Signals, EEG/ECG, energy and finance forecasting, multimodal medical/industrial problems.
avoid: Avoid a hybrid when a tuned gradient-boosting or single transformer baseline matches it.

qa.q: How can wavelet decomposition leak information?
qa.a: Wavelet/EMD transforms of the full series use future samples when computing coefficients near the boundary; training windows then contain information from the test period. Apply the decomposition causally within each window or fold.
